title: Anyone can read a table you didn't make public
what: Your database answers anonymous visitors with rows from a table that gaugeline.access.json doesn't list as public.
why: The project's public key is in your site's code by design, so anyone can use it to download every row of that table: orders, emails, whatever it holds.
fix: Turn on row level security for the table and add a policy that allows only what visitors need, or mark the table public in gaugeline.access.json if it really is.
tech: Supabase: the exposed tables from PostgREST's OpenAPI description (GET /rest/v1/), then one HEAD /rest/v1/<table>?select=* per table with the anon key and Prefer: count=exact (at most 20); the count comes from Content-Range and no row is downloaded. Readable and empty is not a finding

title: A signed-in user can read other people's rows
what: Signed in as a test user, Gaugeline can read rows of a table that belong to someone else, by the owner column set in gaugeline.access.json.
why: Any customer who signs up can read every other customer's records, and nobody sees it from the site.
fix: Change the table's read policy so a user sees only rows where the owner column is their own id (auth.uid()).
tech: Supabase: per configured test user and per table with an owner column, one HEAD /rest/v1/<table>?select=*&<owner>=neq.<user id> with that user's token and Prefer: count=exact; a count above 0 is a finding. Tokens come from the environment and are only ever sent in the Authorization header

title: The app this page links to isn't in the store
what: An App Store or Google Play link on the page names an app the store no longer has.
why: Visitors who tap "Get the app" land on an error page. Apps disappear when they are renamed, moved to a new developer account or pulled.
fix: Link to the app's current store page, or remove the link if the app is gone.
tech: the iTunes Lookup API returns no result for the id (in the link's storefront and in the US), or the Google Play listing answers 404. A 429 or a regional-only app is could-not-check, not dead

title: Links on this page go nowhere
what: Links to other pages on the site return an error (404, 410 or 5xx).
why: Visitors who click hit a dead end, and search engines take broken links as a sign the site is neglected.
fix: Point each link at the page's current address, or remove it. When a page moved, add a 301 redirect from the old address.
tech: a sampled same-site a[href] ends in 4xx or 5xx. 401, 403, 429 and 503 with Retry-After are refusals: listed as could not check, never broken. A 200 page that says "not found" (a soft 404) is out of scope

title: This page tells Google to show a different page
what: The page's canonical tag names a different address as the real one.
why: Search engines treat the page as a copy, so it may never appear in results.
fix: Give each page a canonical tag that points at its own address. Shared SEO components are the usual cause.
tech: <link rel="canonical"> on the page points at another URL

title: Nothing is left, but the page still looks open for orders
what: Your remaining capacity (dishes for tonight, seats, tickets) is zero, and the order page does not say it is sold out.
why: Customers keep ordering or paying for something you cannot make. Each one is a refund, an apology and a bad review.
fix: Show the sold-out message from the same number that counts what is left, and remove the order button when it reaches zero. If the evidence says a cache served the page, purge it after the count changes.
tech: for each capacity rule in gaugeline.switches.json, the remaining count is read from its source (a published Sanity field or a one-row query through the read-only database source); when it is zero or below, each whenZero.pageSays page must say its phrase (case-insensitive, accents and spacing ignored, per language where given) in the page as sent without JavaScript; the evidence says whether the page still has a form; a page that answers 404, a source or a page that cannot be read is could not check (the link checks report dead pages); the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page

title: The site's certificate expires soon
what: The https certificate the site presented expires in under 21 days (fix soon) or under 7 (fix first), or has expired.
why: When it lapses, every browser shows a full-page security warning instead of the site, and most visitors leave.
fix: Renew it, or find why automatic renewal stopped (a DNS change at cutover often breaks the renewal check). Domain registration expiry is a separate date: check it at your registrar.
tech: Read from the TLS connection of the page's own GET: no extra request. Days left = whole days until notAfter, by the run's clock. Plain http, or a certificate that failed verification, gives nothing here. Domain registration expiry needs registrar access and is not checked

title: A form sends details over an insecure connection
what: A form, its iframe, its embed script or its tracking script loads over plain http on an https page.
why: Browsers may block it on a secure page, and what people type isn't encrypted.
fix: Use https for the form, the tracker domain and the tracking script (pd.js for Pardot).
tech: http:// in a form action, a recognised iframe src, an embed script src or a tracking script src on an https page; the code inside an inline script is not read

title: Leads from this form arrive without where they came from
what: A form from Pardot, HubSpot or Marketo is on the page, but that service's tracking code is not.
why: The service can't connect a new lead to the ad, email or search that brought them.
fix: Add the service's tracking code to every page that has its form (for Pardot: Account Engagement Settings, Domain Management, Tracking Code Generator).
tech: A form or iframe of Pardot, HubSpot or Marketo in the HTML, and no script of that service's tracking code anywhere in it (pi.pardot.com/pd.js or piAId, js.hs-scripts.com or _hsq, munchkin.js or Munchkin.init); Web-to-Lead, Formstack and Typeform have no tracking script and are skipped; a form drawn by JavaScript is could-not-check; code a tag manager adds at run time is not seen

title: Leads have stopped arriving
what: The CRM was getting new leads every few days, and none has been created for several days, while the form is still on the page.
why: A form can load, accept the visitor's details and thank them while the lead goes nowhere: a changed field, an expired integration user, a full queue. Nobody sees it until the phone stays quiet.
fix: Submit the form yourself with a test lead (your own, in a sandbox if you have one), see whether it reaches the CRM, and check the form's connection to Salesforce and the integration user's access.
tech: Through Salesforce's read-only MCP server (soqlQuery on Lead: COUNT and MAX(CreatedDate) since 14 days ago, or four times quietDays if longer): no lead created for quietDays whole days (default 3) after at least 5 in the lookback, on a page that has a form or embed from Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot, Formstack, Marketo or Typeform; a page with no recognised form, or too few leads to call it quiet, is could-not-check

title: A data assertion found rows that should not exist
what: A query you wrote in gaugeline.sources.json to return nothing returned rows: two bookings in one slot, a paid order with no matching payment, a product with no price id.
why: These are the problems a customer finds before you do. No page looks wrong yet, so a check of the page cannot see them, but the next person to book, pay or order runs into one.
fix: Read the rows in the evidence and correct them in the database, or fix the code that wrote them, then run again. If the rule itself is wrong, change the assertion's query.
tech: each assertion is one SELECT that should return no rows, run through the read-only database connector (a statement classifier, BEGIN READ ONLY with a statement timeout and a 5,000 row cap, and the database role); any row is a finding with the assertion's own severity and title, and the evidence is its id, the row count and the allow-listed evidence columns of the first 20 rows; a query that could not run (database down, timeout, wrong evidence column) is could not check, never a pass

title: The numbers on this page are older than they should be
what: The page says when its data was last updated, and that time is older than the limit you set for it while the data is expected to move.
why: A sync that stopped fails quietly: the page keeps showing last week's numbers, and nobody notices until a visitor or a customer does.
fix: Find out why the sync stopped (the evidence says whether the source is just as old), or why the page is not rebuilt after it runs. Then check the stamp itself is generated from the data, not typed or built once.
tech: for each rule with a stamp in gaugeline.freshness.json, the stamp is read from the page as sent, without JavaScript (the selector's datetime, content or named attribute, else its text; else the structured data property) in the stamp's own time zone, else the file's timeZone; it is older than maxAge only when it is older at every instant the stamp could mean (a date alone is a whole day, a time with no zone and no timeZone could be any zone, 3 hours ago is a span of an hour); the rule is checked only in the months of activeWhen, in the site's time zone, and a rule that is not active is listed as could not check, not passed; when the rule also has a source and the page is behind it by more than maxLag, data-behind-source reports that cause instead, so each cause has one finding; a stamp that cannot be read or is undecided is could not check; the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page

title: Private-looking content is in a public Sanity dataset
what: The Sanity dataset your images come from answers without a token, and it has document types that sound like people's details: orders, inquiries, customers, bookings.
why: Anyone can download those documents with one request: names, emails and whatever else the forms collect.
fix: Make the dataset private in sanity.io/manage today and give the site a read token, or move those types to a private dataset.
tech: As dataset-public, and a type name whose last word is in checks/leaks/private-types.ts (order, inquiry, submission, customer and others); only the type names are read, never the documents. dataset-public is not also reported

title: Unpublished work is in the live page
what: The published HTML carries Sanity draft document ids (drafts.…) or a preview-mode banner.
why: Drafts are work nobody approved: prices, announcements or pages that weren't meant to be public yet, readable by anyone who opens the page source.
fix: Build the live site with the published perspective (no drafts), turn preview mode off for public requests, and rebuild.
tech: Ids matching drafts.<id> in attribute values or as string values inside JSON script blocks (application/json, ld+json, __NEXT_DATA__), not in prose; or visible text such as Preview mode or Exit preview. Only the count and the first id are reported, never document content

title: This page has two titles
what: The HTML has more than one title element (titles inside SVG images do not count).
why: Search engines pick one, not always the one you meant, so the result shows the wrong title. It usually means two SEO components both render one.
fix: Keep one <title> in the head. Remove the one a theme, plugin or layout adds on top of your SEO component.
tech: more than one <title> element outside <svg>

title: Your domain doesn't say who may send its email
what: The domain receives email but publishes no SPF record listing the services allowed to send mail as it.
why: Mail you send (receipts, booking confirmations) is more likely to land in spam, and anyone can send mail that claims to be from you.
fix: Add one TXT record at the domain starting v=spf1 that includes each service that sends your mail (your email host, your newsletter tool), ending -all or ~all.
tech: Public DNS only (node:dns/promises, TXT and MX): MX records exist and are not a null MX, and no TXT record at the host (without www.) starts with v=spf1. No mail server is contacted

title: The page and the calendar disagree about an event
what: An event in the page's structured data has a different start time, name or place than the .ics calendar entry on the same day.
why: Search results, the page and guests' phone calendars each show one of the two versions, so some guests turn up at the wrong time.
fix: Correct whichever is wrong, then generate both from one source so they cannot drift.
tech: Event JSON-LD and an .ics occurrence on the same local date: matched by normalised name, then start time and location compared; a lone occurrence that day with another name is reported as renamed

title: The page still promotes an event that already happened
what: An event in the page's structured data, or a card marked as the next or upcoming event, is dated before now.
why: Guests plan around the date on the page. A night that already happened, still shown as next, sends people to a closed room or to a different night.
fix: Update the card and the structured data when an event ends. Generating both from the calendar keeps them current.
tech: an Event's endDate (or startDate when there is none) is before the run time, or a next/upcoming element's time[datetime] is; dates are read in the venue's time zone

title: A fact about your business differs between pages
what: A phone number, opening hours, payment handle or price you declared shows a different value somewhere on the site, in the text, a link or the structured data.
why: Customers call the old number, turn up at the old time or send money to a mistyped handle. Search engines show whichever version they read.
fix: Correct each place the evidence names. Better, render the fact from one source so the pages cannot drift.
tech: every occurrence (visible text by pattern or selector, links, JSON-LD; not image descriptions) equals the declared value in gaugeline.facts.json. "$5" = "$5.00", "5pm" = "5:00 PM", handle case ignored; a value that doesn't parse is unchecked

title: A payment link goes nowhere
what: A Cash App or Venmo link on the site answers with an error: the profile it names doesn't exist.
why: Customers who tap Pay land on an error, or worse, find a look-alike profile and pay a stranger.
fix: Correct the handle in the link, and check it by opening the link on a phone.
tech: cash.app/$handle and venmo.com/(u/)handle links on the pages checked are requested (HEAD, then GET on 405/501) and answer 4xx or 5xx; at most 5, and only the address the page names is sent (ADR-0004)

title: The feed this page advertises is broken
what: The page links to an RSS or Atom feed that returns an error (4xx or 5xx).
why: Feed readers, podcast apps and newsletter tools that follow the site stop getting new posts, usually without anyone noticing.
fix: Restore the feed at that address, or update the link rel="alternate" tag to where the feed lives now.
tech: an advertised feed returns 4xx or 5xx

title: A form now sends to a different service
what: A form that sent its entries to one service (HubSpot, say) now posts to another.
why: Leads go somewhere nobody is watching, or to an account you don't control, from the moment it changed.
fix: Check who changed the form's action; point it back at your service, or update your follow-up to the new one.
tech: With --since last only: the same form key (id, else name, else position) now posts to a host in a different provider row of the frozen table; position keys can swap and read as a change

title: A download meant for customers is handed to anyone
what: A download route returns its file to a request with no session and no purchase.
why: A route that protects a paid file should refuse, or send the visitor to sign in. If it returns the file, everyone who has the address gets it for free, and the address is easy to find in the page, in a search engine or in a customer's email.
fix: Check the purchase inside the route before it answers, then hand back a short-lived signed link instead of the file itself. A route with no session should answer 401, 403 or a redirect to sign in.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: one anonymous GET per route (no cookie, no Authorization, no Referer, no compression), the status and headers, then at most 1,024 bytes of the body and the connection is closed; the route is a same-site link whose path contains download, file, deliver or export or sits under /api/, or a route file given with --routes (app/**/route.ts, pages/api/**) whose path says the same; a dynamic segment is asked only for an address seen in a link and ids are never guessed; at most 10 routes, in sorted order, the rest named; a finding is status 200 with a file content type or Content-Disposition attachment and first bytes that are not HTML (%PDF, PK, ID3 and a few other signatures are read); 401, 403, 404, a redirect to a sign-in address and a 200 HTML page pass; a redirect elsewhere is followed one hop; the body and the query string are never stored, logged or printed

title: Hidden text on the page gives orders to AI assistants
what: Text that visitors can't see, or a comment in the page's code, speaks to an AI assistant (for example 'ignore previous instructions').
why: It is one of the commonest signs a site has been tampered with. Assistants and crawlers read text that visitors never see, so whoever planted it can steer what they say about your business.
fix: Find where the text comes from (a plugin, a theme file, a content field or an injected script) and remove it. Then find out how it got there, and change the passwords and keys that could have put it there.
tech: text under hidden, aria-hidden, display:none, visibility:hidden, font-size:0, opacity:0, an off-screen left or top, text coloured as its own background, noscript, or an HTML comment, containing a phrase from data/ai-directives.json

title: Unlaunched pages are in your sitemap
what: The sitemap lists addresses in a section gaugeline.hidden.json says is hidden until launch.
why: The sitemap is the list you hand to search engines: they will crawl and index the section before anyone meant it to be public.
fix: Leave the hidden section out of the sitemap until launch, usually a filter on the same flag that hides the pages.
tech: Every address listed by the sitemaps read (robots.txt's, /sitemap.xml, one level of sitemap index), matched against the hidden path globs

title: An unlaunched page can be indexed
what: An address in a hidden section, found in the sitemap or through a link, answers 200 with no noindex and no login.
why: Anyone who finds it can read it, and search engines can list it before launch.
fix: Send noindex (X-Robots-Tag or a robots meta tag) on the hidden section until launch, or put it behind a login.
tech: Hidden addresses from the sitemaps and from hiddenLinks, at most 5, fetched once with GET for the status, X-Robots-Tag and meta robots only (nothing else of the page is read); 401, 403, 404 or a redirect out of the section is a pass

title: A public page links to an unlaunched section
what: A public page links to an address in a hidden section, directly or through a redirect.
why: Visitors and search engines follow the link into pages nobody meant to show yet, usually from a shared menu, footer or related-posts block.
fix: Hide the link behind the same flag as the section, or remove it until launch.
tech: Links on the checked page and the run's other public pages whose address matches a hidden path glob, and sampled same-site links whose redirects end in one

title: Your whole site exists at two addresses
what: Both www and the bare domain load the site, instead of one redirecting to the other.
why: Search engines can split your ranking between two copies of every page.
fix: Pick one address and 301-redirect the other to it at your host or DNS provider.
tech: the alternate host returns 200 instead of 301

title: This page's HTML is enormous
what: The HTML of the page alone is over 2 MB, before any image, script or stylesheet.
why: Phones on slow connections wait seconds before anything shows, and search engines may stop reading the page before the end.
fix: Find what fills the HTML: usually a framework data payload, inlined SVG or CSS, or a long list rendered in full. Load it on demand or paginate it.
tech: the UTF-8 HTML body is over 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes); html-heavy is not reported for the same page

title: Your calendar shows the wrong hour on some phones
what: Events in your .ics calendar have a start time with no time zone (no TZID and no Z).
why: Phones read such a time in the guest's own zone, so anyone in another zone, or travelling, sees the event at the wrong hour.
fix: Give each DTSTART a time zone, for example DTSTART;TZID=America/Los_Angeles:20261112T190000. Most calendar exports have a time zone setting.
tech: a VEVENT's DTSTART has neither TZID nor a trailing Z (a floating time, RFC 5545 §3.3.5); all-day VALUE=DATE events are not reported

title: Some images on this page don't load
what: An image on the site (or the original behind a Next.js /_next/image address) returns an error.
why: Visitors see an empty box or a broken-image icon where a product photo or a diagram should be.
fix: Upload the image again, or point the img at its current address. For /_next/image, check the file named by url= exists.
tech: a sampled same-site img src answers 4xx or 5xx (images on other hosts are not requested); a refusal (401, 403, 429, 503 with Retry-After) is listed as could not check

title: The page carries text in invisible characters
what: Characters from the Unicode tag block are in the page's text. They show nothing on screen but each one stands for a letter.
why: They have no ordinary use on a web page, and AI assistants can read the message they spell. Seeing them is a sign of tampering or of text pasted in from somewhere untrusted.
fix: Delete them from the field or file they came from, then check who and what can edit that content.
tech: code points U+E0000 to U+E007F in a text node or comment, other than the England, Scotland and Wales flag emoji (U+1F3F4, tag letters, U+E007F)

title: An item that is sold out or off the menu is still listed
what: An item your database or CMS marks as unavailable (86'd, sold out, off the menu) is still on a page that lists items, or in the page's Menu structured data.
why: Customers order or plan around something you cannot serve, and search results and assistants repeat it from the structured data long after the page is fixed.
fix: Build the menu pages and the Menu structured data from the same list that holds the availability, so an item that is off cannot be rendered. If the evidence says a cache served the page, purge it.
tech: for each availability rule in gaugeline.switches.json, the unavailable item names are read from the source (a Sanity list of names or one column of a query through the read-only database source) and looked for in the text of each mustNotAppearOn page, as sent without JavaScript and with hidden elements left out: an item is found when its words stand on their own in a row, ignoring case, accents and plural endings, at the start of a line or after punctuation (so Tamal is not found in Tamal de rajas); with alsoIn menu-jsonld the names of MenuItem nodes in the structured data of those pages and of the page checked are compared the same way; the evidence gives both spellings when they differ and adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page; an unreadable source or page is could not check (one that answers 404 lists nothing)

title: Structured data points at pages that don't exist
what: Addresses on the site named in the page's structured data (a product URL, an image, a logo) return an error.
why: Search engines use these addresses for rich results. A dead product or image address can drop the rich result entirely.
fix: Update the structured data to the current addresses. Generated structured data usually means a stale CMS field or a renamed route.
tech: same-site http(s) strings inside JSON-LD answer 4xx or 5xx; at most 12 are requested, the first 12 in document order

title: This page's structured data is broken
what: A structured data block (script type="application/ld+json") is not valid JSON.
why: Search engines ignore the whole block, so prices, reviews, FAQs or opening hours in it never reach the results.
fix: Fix the JSON in that block: usually a trailing comma, an unescaped quote or a template that printed nothing. Paste it into a JSON validator to find the line.
tech: JSON.parse fails on a script type="application/ld+json" block (one finding per block)

title: Prices differ between language versions
what: The same item (matched by its structured data sku, or name) shows a different price on another language version of the page.
why: Customers see one price and pay another, or compare the two versions and stop trusting either.
fix: Update the price on every version, ideally from one product record. A version that was copied and translated keeps last month's price.
tech: Product or Offer price in JSON-LD (then the configured priceSelector; never free text) differs for one sku across versions; "$12", "12 USD" and "$12.00" are equal

title: A listing shows different opening hours
what: On at least one day, the hours on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing are not the hours on your site.
why: People decide where to go from the hours in the search result. A listing that says you close at 10 when you stay open until 2 loses the late crowd, and one that says you open early sends people to a locked door.
fix: Make the hours the same in the listing's own dashboard and on the site. Decide which one is right first, then fix the other.
tech: both sides become seven lists of intervals in the venue's local time (a close after midnight belongs to the day it opens, split shifts stay split) and each day the site states is compared; a day the site does not mention is not; a day missing from a listing that gave hours is closed; the site's hours are the hours fact in gaugeline.facts.json, else LocalBusiness openingHours or openingHoursSpecification

title: A listing still uses your old business name
what: The name on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing is not the name your site uses.
why: Most people find a bar or a clinic through the listing, not the website. If it still shows a name you retired, they search for the wrong thing and doubt that the place is the one they want.
fix: Change the name in the listing's own dashboard (Google Business Profile, Yelp for Business, Apple Business Connect) to the one on your site, or fix the site if the listing is right.
tech: the listing's name, normalised (case, accents, punctuation and a leading or trailing "The" ignored), is neither equal to the site's name nor the site's name with words around it; the site's name is the text fact "name" in gaugeline.facts.json, else the LocalBusiness name in structured data; permanently closed listings are not compared

title: A listing shows a different phone number
what: The phone number on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing is not the one on your site.
why: The phone number on the listing is the one people tap from the search result. A wrong one sends bookings and orders to a dead line or a stranger.
fix: Update the phone number in the listing's own dashboard, or on the site if the listing is the right one.
tech: the digits of the listing's phone number (a leading +1 or 1 on a North American number ignored) differ from the digits of the site's: the phone fact in gaugeline.facts.json, else the LocalBusiness telephone in structured data; numbers that are not 7 to 15 digits are not compared

title: A listing links to the wrong place
what: The website link on a listing, or in a social bio, leads to an old domain, to a page that no longer works, or through a long chain of redirects.
why: The website button on the listing is how a guest reaches the menu and the booking form. When it points at an old domain that lapses, or a page you deleted, every one of those visits ends in an error.
fix: Set the listing's website to your site's current address, in the listing's own dashboard or in the bio.
tech: the link is opened with GET (at most 8 distinct links, one request each): it is wrong when it cannot be opened, answers 400 or above, is on a different host from the checked site (www ignored) even if it redirects there, or takes 3 redirects or more; a link-in-bio page is right when it lands on the site or links to it; Yelp does not return a website, so it is not compared

title: Test content is on the live site
what: The page's main content shows test or sample content: a test product, a sample post, John Doe, an example.com email address or a 555 phone number.
why: Unlike placeholder copy, a visitor can act on it: buy the test product, email the example address or call the fake number.
fix: Delete or unpublish the test entries in the CMS or shop, and replace sample contact details with real ones.
tech: main content (code and pre ignored) contains "test product", "sample product", "sample post", "sample page", "test post", "hello world!", "john doe", "jane doe", "john smith example", "your name here", "product name here", an @example.com/.org/.net address, or a 555 phone number (English lists)

title: Anyone can switch on draft mode
what: A draft or preview route on this Next.js site turns draft mode on for a request that carries no secret.
why: Anyone who visits that address sees unpublished content (prices, announcements, pages nobody approved) as if it were live.
fix: Make the route check a secret (compare a token from the request with one from your environment) before it enables draft mode, and return 401 otherwise.
tech: Next.js sites only: one GET per conventional route (/api/draft, /api/preview, /api/draft-mode/enable, /api/enable-draft), no secret sent or guessed; a Set-Cookie of __prerender_bypass or __next_preview_data on any hop is a finding

title: The live site points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this Next.js site gives a preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up.
fix: Build the site's base address from the production domain (often NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL set only for preview builds), and rebuild.
tech: Next.js sites served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev

title: This page asks search engines not to list it
what: The page has a robots meta tag containing noindex.
why: If that isn't on purpose, the page is invisible in search.
fix: Remove noindex from pages you want found.
tech: <meta name="robots" content="noindex">

title: A page from the last run is gone
what: An address the last run read (saved with --since last) now answers 404 or 410, or redirects to a different page; the evidence says where it now leads.
why: Links from other sites, bookmarks and search results still point at the old address: a page that went missing loses them all, and one redirected to the wrong place loses them more slowly.
fix: Put the page back, or redirect it with a 301 to the page that replaces it. A page removed on purpose goes under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json.
tech: With --since last only. Each saved address is taken from this run's pages when it was read anyway, else requested once with GET. A redirect that ends on the same path (a trailing slash, https) is not gone. A server error or refusal is could not check. On a first run: could not check

title: A page lost content since the last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, a page's main content fell by more than 40%, or a whole section (a heading and everything under it) is gone.
why: The page still loads, so nothing else notices: a template change, a failed import or an editor's mistake can empty a page that visitors and search engines relied on.
fix: Restore what went missing, or list the page under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json with the reason when the loss was meant.
tech: With --since last only. Words are counted in the main content (main, else body) with the header, footer, navigation and asides left out, so a menu change doesn't count. A section is an h2 or h3; a heading gone is a section gone. Exactly 40% fewer words is not a loss. On a first run: could not check

title: Page 2 of this list shows page 1 again
what: A later page of the list answers, and its main text is identical to the first page's.
why: The page parameter is ignored, so every older item is unreachable for visitors and search engines, and the copies count as duplicate pages.
fix: Make the list read the page number (often a query parameter the framework drops, or a cache that ignores the query string).

title: Page 2 of this list has no address
what: The page shows page numbers or a next or load-more control, and the HTML has no address for page 2: the control only works with JavaScript.
why: Search engines don't click buttons, so everything after the first page of the list is never found, and nobody can link to it.

title: A file people pay for is on a public address
what: A page that shows a price links straight to a file (pdf, zip, epub, mp3, mp4, docx or xlsx) on a public asset store.
why: Asset stores are world-readable by design. Anyone who has the address, or finds it in the page's source or a search engine, can download the file without paying.

title: A payment handle differs from yours
what: A page shows a Zelle, Cash App, Venmo or PayPal handle that is not the one you set for that service.
why: Customers who copy it send their money to someone else, and nobody finds out until you ask where the money went.
fix: Correct the handle where it is written (usually one shared footer or CMS field), then open it on a phone to check it is yours.

title: A payment detail you didn't set is on the site
what: A page shows a payment handle for a service you didn't set up, or a Square or Stripe payment link that isn't one of yours.
why: An old account, a copied template or a stranger's handle takes customers' money where you can't see it.
fix: Remove it, or add it to gaugeline.payments.json if it really is yours.

title: A payment link no longer works
what: A Square or Stripe payment link on the site answers 404, or shows the provider's page for a link that has been turned off.
why: Customers who are ready to pay hit a dead end, and most of them don't come back to try another way.
fix: Make a new payment link in Square or Stripe and replace the old one everywhere it appears.

title: Assistants find two different names for your business
what: The business name in the page's structured data and the title of /llms.txt are not the same name.
why: Assistants match a question to a business by name. Two names can make them treat one business as two, or quote the wrong one.
fix: Use the same business name in the LocalBusiness structured data and as the first heading of llms.txt.

title: Your robots.txt tells every search engine to stay away
what: robots.txt has a group for every crawler (User-agent: *) that disallows the whole site.
why: Search engines stop crawling the site, so new pages never appear and old ones fade out of results.
fix: Remove the Disallow: / line from the User-agent: * group, or replace it with the paths you mean to hide. This line is often left over from a staging site.

title: The page address returns app data, not a page
what: A normal request to the page returns the framework's data format (text/x-component), or HTML with no readable words while the prefetch request returns the page's data.
why: Search engines and visitors without JavaScript get nothing to read: the page can drop out of search while every check that loads it in a browser looks fine.

title: Your organization has more than one identity in structured data
what: The Organization or WebSite @id differs from the one in your schema guide, or differs from page to page.
why: Search engines join structured data across pages by @id. Two ids make two organizations, splitting what is known about yours.

tech: an Organization or WebSite @id (compared after resolving and trimming a trailing slash) differs from organizationId/websiteId, or, with no guide, differs between the sampled pages

title: A private key is in your site's JavaScript
what: A secret key (a Stripe secret or restricted key, a Sanity token, or a long random value named like a secret) is in JavaScript the site sends to every visitor.
why: Anyone can read it in their browser and use it as you: take payments, read customer data or change your content.
fix: Revoke the key in the provider's dashboard now, make a new one, and keep it on the server: never in code the browser loads.

title: Your sitemap lists pages that don't exist
what: Pages listed in the sitemap return an error (4xx or 5xx).
why: The sitemap is where you tell search engines which pages matter. Dead entries waste their visits and make them trust the sitemap less.
fix: Remove the dead addresses from the sitemap, or restore the pages. A generated sitemap usually means a deleted page is still in the CMS or the route list.

title: Your staging site can be found by search engines
what: staging.<your domain> answers with a page and doesn't ask search engines to stay away.
why: Search engines can index the unfinished copy alongside the real site, with old prices, test content or duplicate pages competing with yours.
fix: Put the staging site behind a password, or send X-Robots-Tag: noindex (or <meta name="robots" content="noindex">) on every staging page.

title: Hidden editing characters leaked onto the live site
what: The title, a meta tag or the structured data contains invisible characters: Unicode tag characters or long runs of zero-width characters, the kind a CMS preview (such as Sanity's stega) adds.
why: They are invisible to you but not to everyone else: search results, share previews and copied text carry them, and they can break string comparisons and structured data.
fix: Turn stega encoding off for production builds (in Sanity, set stega: false outside preview) and strip it from fields that end up in metadata.

title: This live site is using Stripe's test key
what: The page, or a script on the same site, carries a Stripe test publishable key (it starts pk_test_) and the page is not on a hosting provider's preview address.
why: A checkout built on a test key looks like it works and takes no real money: every order a customer places goes nowhere, and no card is charged.
fix: In Stripe, switch to live mode, copy the live publishable key (pk_live_) and put it where the site reads its key, then redeploy and place one small real order to be sure.

title: A switch is off but the site still links to what it controls
what: You turned a feature off (pre-orders, online ordering, bookings), and a page still has a link to the page that feature runs on.
why: Visitors click the link, land on a page that no longer works or takes orders you cannot fill, and call or leave. A cached or hard-coded link is the usual cause: the menu and the header were built before the switch was flipped.
fix: Make every link to the controlled page depend on the same switch (in Sanity or the database), or remove the link. If the evidence says the answer came from a cache, purge the cache after the switch changes.

title: Links still point at a temporary address
what: The page, on your own domain, links to a hosting provider's temporary address (vercel.app, netlify.app or pages.dev).
why: Those addresses are previews: they can show old content, ask for a login, or vanish when the preview is cleaned up, and search engines split your site between two names.
fix: Change each link to the same path on your domain. Search the code and the CMS for the temporary name: it is often in a menu, a button or an environment variable.

title: Google sees an almost empty page
what: Fewer than 60 words exist in the page before JavaScript runs, outside the header, nav and footer.
why: Many crawlers and AI tools read the page without running JavaScript, so they see almost nothing.
fix: Render the main content on the server. In Next.js, keep it out of client-only components and Suspense boundaries that wait for the browser.
tech: word count of server-rendered HTML

title: A planned page doesn't exist on the preview
what: A page the plan lists returns 404 (or 410) on the preview given with --base.
why: A planned page that doesn't exist at cutover loses every visitor and link meant for it.
fix: Build the page, or take the row out of the plan if it was dropped.
tech: Each planned path on --base fetched once with GET; 404 or 410 on the final hop. One finding per path, with every row on it

title: A canonical points somewhere other than the planned page
what: The page's canonical names another address, often the legacy one, instead of the planned page.
why: Search engines index the canonical: the new page won't be listed, the old address will.
fix: Point the canonical at the page's own planned address on production.
tech: The canonical's path (lower case, no trailing slash) against the row's path, on the preview's host or the plan's production host, with or without www

title: An old address doesn't redirect
what: An old address in the plan's Legacy URL column still answers 200 or 404 on the preview instead of redirecting.
why: The old address's rankings and links go nowhere: a 404 loses them, a page left in place competes with the new one.
fix: Add a 301 from the old address to the row's new one. A meta refresh or JavaScript redirect isn't one.
tech: The legacy address (its path and query, moved onto --base) fetched with GET; the first hop isn't a 3xx. A 200 with a meta refresh or a location assignment is reported with that hint

title: An old address redirects with a temporary status
what: An old address redirects with 302, 303 or 307, or with 308 to the wrong place.
why: A temporary redirect tells search engines the old address is coming back, so its rankings may not move to the new page.
fix: Make it a 301. A 308 is permanent too and is accepted when it goes to the right place.
tech: The status of the first hop. 308 to the planned page is accepted, with a note on stderr

title: An old address redirects somewhere the plan doesn't say
what: An old address redirects, but not to the page the plan says it should.
why: The old address's visitors and rankings land on the wrong page, and the planned page starts from nothing.
fix: Point the redirect at the row's URL. Right path on www instead of the bare host (or the reverse) costs another hop.
tech: The trail's final address (or where the last hop points, when it leaves the preview): its path against the row's, on the preview's host or exactly the plan's

title: One old address is claimed by two rows
what: One old address is the Legacy URL of two rows that plan different pages.
why: An address can redirect to one place only: one of the two rows won't get its traffic, and no crawl will show it.
fix: Decide which page the old address goes to and remove it from the other row.
tech: Legacy URL cells split on line breaks and commas, keyed by path and query (lower case, no trailing slash); two rows with different addresses on one key. Needs no --base

title: A page that exists today has no row in the plan
what: An address in the --live export (a crawl, a sitemap, a Search Console export or a list) has no row in the plan and no Legacy URL pointing at it.
why: A page that ranks today and has nowhere to go at launch loses its traffic and links: the most expensive thing on a migration.
fix: Add a row for the page, or put its address in the Legacy URL of the row that replaces it.
tech: Live paths (lower case, no trailing slash, no query) against a Set of every row path and legacy path; assets, feeds, ?page= and --ignore globs left out. Sorted by clicks, impressions or position when the export has them. Three or more that differ from planned rows only by a leading prefix are one finding

title: A menu item has no page in the plan
what: An item in a menu tab of the plan workbook has no page row in the page plan, and no page shares a distinctive word with it (or several do).
why: The menu will link to a page nobody planned: it gets built late, without a title or keyword, or the link goes nowhere.
fix: Add a row for the page, or rename the menu item to the page it means. A menu heading with no page of its own can have a row with no URL.

title: Two rows in the plan share one address
what: Two or more rows of the plan give the same address (path and #section), so only one of those pages can exist.
why: The pages compete for one address: one gets built, the other is lost, and whichever wins gets the wrong title, heading and redirects.
fix: Give each planned page its own address, or merge the rows into one page.
tech: Rows grouped by host without www. and path in lower case, no trailing slash or query, plus #fragment when there is one; an anchor row and its page row differ by the fragment. One finding per group, with every line

title: A printed address doesn't land on a page
what: A printed address (a QR code, a flyer, a short link) ends in a 4xx or 5xx, or no longer answers on the http:// that was printed.
why: A printed code can't be reprinted when a page moves: everyone who scans it gets an error.
fix: Add a redirect from the printed address to the page it was for, and answer on http if http was printed.
tech: The printed URL fetched as printed with GET; the trail's last hop is 400 or above. A printed http:// that refuses the connection while https:// answers is reported here

title: A printed address lands somewhere it shouldn't
what: A printed address lands somewhere other than its expectedDestination, or stops on an interstitial page that sends people on.
why: People scanned a code for one thing and got another, or a page they have to wait through.
fix: Point the printed address's redirect at the expected page, and make a short link redirect with a 301 rather than show its own page.
tech: The trail's final address against expectedDestination (host without www, path without trailing slash). A 200 with a meta refresh or a location assignment and no redirect is an interstitial

title: Campaign tags are lost
what: A redirect between the ad and its landing page drops utm_source, utm_campaign, gclid or fbclid.
why: The visit arrives with no sign of the ad that paid for it, so the report credits nobody, the campaign looks like it did nothing and the money is spent without a way to learn from it.
fix: Make the redirect pass the query string on, or point the ad straight at the final address.

title: The page doesn't load
what: An ad sends people to a page that answers 404, 410 or a server error, or that cannot be reached at all.
why: Everyone clicking that ad lands on an error, so every click is paid for and nobody can buy, book or call.
fix: Bring the page back, or redirect its address to the page that replaced it, then check the ad's link. Pause the ad until it works.

title: The advertised product is sold out
what: An ad sends people to a Shopify product page where every variant is sold out.
why: Each click is paid for by someone who wants to buy and cannot, so the money buys nothing until the product is back.
fix: Pause the ad or point it at a product that is in stock, and turn it back on when the product returns. If some sizes are out, say so in the ad.

title: A fulfillment product has variants that cannot be made
what: A Printful product matched to a product on your website has a variant that is not synced.
why: Printful cannot make an order for a variant whose design is not matched to a printable item, so a customer can pay for something that is never printed.
fix: In Printful, open the product and finish syncing the variants listed, or remove them from the store and from the website.
tech: a matched Printful product with at least one sync_variants entry whose synced is false; runs when Printful returned data; the variants are listed by SKU, or by id when there is none, at most 10 and then a count of the rest; an unmatched Printful product is not reported here; with Sanity not read it is reported from the Printful list alone

title: A website product is archived in checkout
what: The Stripe product matched to a product on your website is archived.
why: Stripe will not sell an archived product, so the page invites a purchase that checkout turns down.
fix: Unarchive the product in Stripe if it is still on sale, or take it off the website if it is not.
tech: a matched Stripe product with active false; runs when Stripe returned data; an archived Stripe product that nothing matches is not reported (it is not an orphan either); with Sanity not read it is reported from the Stripe list alone; one finding per product with its name and the Sanity and Stripe ids

title: A website product is missing from checkout
what: A product published on your website has no matching product in Stripe.
why: A product people can see but checkout does not know cannot be bought: the button fails, or the order never reaches you. That is lost money from the first visitor.
fix: Create the product in Stripe, or save its Stripe id on the website product so the two are linked. If it is not for sale, unpublish it.

title: Website price disagrees with checkout
what: The price on your website (Sanity) is different from the price Stripe charges for the same product.
why: Customers see one price and pay another, which causes abandoned carts, complaints and refunds.
fix: Decide which system owns the price, usually checkout, and have the other read from it. Until then, change one of the two so they agree.

title: The page sells a plan that is archived in checkout
what: A plan on your page is paired with a Stripe price that has been archived.
why: Visitors can pick the plan, but the price behind it can no longer be used to start a subscription: checkout fails, or an old link keeps charging a price you retired.
fix: Point the page at the plan's current Stripe price, or restore the price in Stripe if it should still be sold. Take the plan off the page if it is gone.

title: A plan bills on a different schedule than the page says
what: The page says a plan bills one way (per month, say) and the matched Stripe price bills another (yearly, or every 3 months), or is not a subscription price at all.
why: A customer who expects 49 a month is charged 588 up front, or the other way round. It is the commonest cause of subscription refunds and chargebacks.
fix: Change the page's wording or pick the Stripe price that bills on the schedule the page promises. Create the missing price in Stripe if there is none.

title: A plan's price on the page differs from checkout
what: The price shown for a plan on your page is different from the Stripe price it is paired with, or the page and Stripe disagree about whether tax is included.
why: Customers see one price and are charged another, which causes abandoned checkouts, complaints and refunds.
fix: Decide which price you mean, then change the other so they agree. If the difference is tax, say on the page whether the price includes it.

title: A field your query asks for is on no document

title: A document type your query asks for has no documents
what: A query in your code asks for a document type, and the dataset has no published documents of it.
why: Either the type was renamed or the content has not been created yet. Every page built from the query is blank, and its fields are not reported separately because none of them can exist.
fix: Check the type's name in the Studio against the one in the query, or publish the documents. A document that is only a draft does not count.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never counted), asking for count(*[_type == T]) and count(*[_type == T && defined(path)]) for each distinct field path, held in a Map from type to a Map from path to an integer; a reference or an array of objects is counted at the field itself (topic, not topic->title); the answer is integers, so no document and no field value is read; count(*[_type == T]) is 0

title: Two documents share a slug
what: Two or more published documents of one type have the same slug.
why: A slug is the address. Only one document can own it, so a page built from the other cannot be reached, or the site shows whichever the query happens to return first.
fix: Open the documents named by their ids in the Studio. Delete the copy you do not want, or give it its own slug.

title: Orders were paid and no receipt went out
