title: A webhook endpoint is not receiving its events
what: An enabled Stripe webhook endpoint has events older than an hour that were never delivered.
why: Stripe tells your site about a payment through a webhook. If the endpoint is down or answering with an error, the payment happened and your site was never told, so no order is recorded, no file is released and no email is sent.
fix: Open the endpoint in the Stripe dashboard, read the failed attempts to see what it answered, fix the route (or the host behind it), then let Stripe retry or resend the events from the dashboard. Gaugeline never replays or retries them.
tech: GET /v1/webhook_endpoints and GET /v1/events with delivery_success=false from the last 30 days; an event counts against an enabled endpoint that takes its type (or *) when it is older than 1 hour and still has pending deliveries, so two endpoints that take the same type are each told about the same event; the evidence is the endpoint's host (never its path, query or secret), the count and the age of the oldest; nothing from an event's payload is read into a result

title: The bare domain and www don't settle on one address
what: Of the bare domain and www, exactly one should answer 200 and the other redirect to it permanently (301 or 308). After cutover, both answer, neither does, or the redirect is temporary.
why: Two live copies split links and ranking between them; a missing one is a dead address for everyone who types it; a temporary redirect tells search engines to keep the old one.
fix: Pick one (most sites use the bare domain or www, either is fine) and redirect the other to it with a 301. Most hosts have a primary-domain setting for this.
tech: GET https://<domain>/ and https://www.<domain>/ through the fetcher, first hop each. Also reported when how either answers changed since the snapshot, with both values

title: The domain's mail records changed at cutover
what: Against the snapshot taken before cutover, the domain's MX records (where its mail is delivered) or its SPF record (who may send as it) are different.
why: A new host's DNS template often replaces the mail records: mail then bounces or goes to an old server, and receipts and confirmations land in spam, with nothing on the site to show it.
fix: Put the old MX and SPF values back unless the move was meant. If it was, list mx or spf under expectedChanges in gaugeline.cutover.json with the reason.
tech: gaugeline cutover --before <file>. MX and TXT (v=spf1) at the domain, compared as sets, so order is not a change. A lookup that failed in either run is could not check, never a change

title: The iPhone app banner promotes a different app
what: The page's Smart App Banner (the apple-itunes-app meta tag) names a different app id than the page's App Store link.
why: Safari shows the banner at the top of the page on iPhone, so visitors install whichever app it names, which here is not the one the page links to.
fix: Set app-id in the apple-itunes-app meta tag to the same id as the App Store link.
tech: <meta name="apple-itunes-app" content="app-id=..."> differs from every apps.apple.com/.../id<digits> link on the page

title: Nothing on the page can be linked to buy
what: A page shows a price and a buy button, but no button is a link with an address or a submit button in a form with an action.
why: Nobody can share a link to the purchase, search engines see no offer, and if the script fails the page is a brochure.
fix: Make the buy button a link to your checkout or payment link, or a submit button in a form that posts to your cart, and let the script improve it from there.
tech: a price (a currency next to a number in the visible text, or an Offer price in the structured data) and at least one button or link whose text matches buy, add to cart, checkout, get it, purchase or download now; none is an a[href] with an address (not empty, #, javascript:, mailto: or tel:) or a submit button in a form with an action or its own formaction; a link to a hosted payment page (Stripe, Square, PayPal.me) anywhere on the page is a pass; the page is read as sent, so a button drawn by a script is not seen

title: A form sends fields the CRM doesn't have
what: A Web-to-Lead form on the page submits field names that are not fields on the Lead object in Salesforce.
why: Salesforce drops what it can't place. The visitor typed it, the form said thanks, and the CRM never got it.
fix: Add the field to Lead in Salesforce and use its name in the form, or remove the input from the form.
tech: The names of every input, select and textarea in each Web-to-Lead form in the HTML (hidden or visible; buttons and files excluded) against the field names and labels of Lead from Salesforce's read-only MCP server (getObjectSchema); Web-to-Lead's own names (first_name, zip, lead_source) are matched to their Lead fields; routing, anti-spam and utm_* names are skipped; custom fields sent by id (00N...) can't be compared and are counted; a form in an iframe or drawn by script is could-not-check

title: Tracking starts after the form loads
what: The service's tracking code comes after its form in the page, or waits for the page to finish loading while the form is an iframe that loads first.
why: Salesforce documents that this can lose first-touch tracking, the referring site and UTM parameters.
fix: Load the tracking script directly in the page head, before the form, not from a window load handler.
tech: Position of the tracking script after the form in document order (counted over every form, iframe and script element), or inline tracking code started by addEventListener("load"), attachEvent("onload") or window.onload while the form is an iframe; no timing is measured, and code a tag manager moves at run time is not seen

title: New leads are arriving without a source
what: Many of the leads created in your CRM since the last run have an empty lead source or campaign field.
why: A lead with no source can't be tied to the ad, email or search that brought it, so the campaign that worked looks the same as the one that didn't.
fix: Make the form send the source: add hidden utm_source and utm_campaign fields, map them to the CRM's lead source or campaign field, and fill the existing records that have none.
tech: Through Salesforce's read-only MCP server (soqlQuery on Lead, newest 200 created since the last run or windowDays ago): leads whose LeadSource, or each field named in sourceFields in gaugeline.crm.json, is null or blank; flagged at 2 or more leads and 10% or more of the sample; evidence is the counts, the field names and up to five record ids, never a name or an email

title: A form has nowhere to put campaign details
what: A form posts leads straight to Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot or Marketo with no hidden campaign fields.
why: Every lead arrives with its campaign, source and ad click blank.
fix: Add hidden utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign and gclid fields, fill them from the address, and map them in the form handler.
tech: A form element posting to Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot or Marketo with no hidden input named utm_*, gclid, a lead source or that service's default mapped field; a visible input does not count; an iframe is another document and is could-not-check

title: The page is behind the data it is built from
what: The source (your database or CMS) has newer data than the page shows, or a figure on the page differs from the same figure in the source.
why: The sync works but the visitor does not see it: a cache or a revalidation setting is serving an old copy, so fixing the sync would change nothing.
fix: Look at how the page is rebuilt after the data changes: its revalidate time, an on-demand revalidation that the sync should call, or a CDN that keeps the old copy. The evidence shows the Age header when a cache served it.
tech: for each rule with a source and maxLag in gaugeline.freshness.json, the newest time is read from the source (a one-row query or a Sanity field) and compared with the page's stamp: reported only when the page is older than the source by more than maxLag at every instant the stamp could mean; for each spot check (up to five per rule) the figure at the selector is compared with the source's figure for the page (a one-row query, or the row whose key column is the last part of the page's address) with exact decimal arithmetic and the tolerance given (an amount or a percentage of the source's figure); an unreadable source, stamp or figure is could not check; the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page

title: Your domain has no DMARC policy
what: There is no DMARC record at _dmarc.<your domain>, so receiving servers have no instruction for mail that fails SPF or DKIM.
why: Mail pretending to be from you is delivered like any other, and large mail providers increasingly expect a DMARC record from anyone who sends.
fix: Add a TXT record at _dmarc.<your domain>: start with v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:<an address you read>, then move to quarantine once the reports look right.
tech: Public DNS only: no TXT record starting v=DMARC1 at _dmarc.<host without www.>. The host is read as given; a parent domain's policy is not looked up

title: Your domain has two SPF records, which cancels both
what: Two or more TXT records at the domain start with v=spf1.
why: Receiving mail servers treat more than one SPF record as an error and ignore all of them, so your mail is checked as if you had none.
fix: Merge them into one record: one v=spf1, every include from both, one -all or ~all at the end.
tech: Public DNS only: the domain has MX records (not a null MX) and two or more TXT records start with v=spf1 (RFC 7208 §4.5: a permerror)

title: An event at your venue lists a different address
what: An event the page says is at the venue (by the venue's name or id) gives a different street address than the venue's own structured data.
why: Maps and search results send guests to the event's address, so a stale one sends them to the wrong door.
fix: Use the venue's own address in each event's location, ideally by referring to the venue's @id instead of repeating it.
tech: Event location names the LocalBusiness (same name or @id) and its address differs by house number or ZIP

title: A click your tracking plan expects isn't reported
what: An element in gaugeline.events.json sends no event when clicked, sends it twice, or sends it without a parameter the plan requires.
why: Tracking breaks quietly when templates change: the report for that menu or button just goes empty, and before-and-after comparisons stop meaning anything.
fix: Restore the click handler or tag for that element, and fill every parameter the plan names (for a menu: link text, destination and parent menu).
tech: Each element a plan line selects (a CSS selector, or every link in nav, header, footer or main; at most 20) is clicked in the rendered page with analytics requests intercepted and never delivered, and dataLayer pushes are read for 1500 ms. One push with the event name and every listed parameter filled passes. Needs a rendered read (G39): until then it is could not check

title: A page is missing a fact it should show
what: A fact you declared must appear on a page (mustAppearOn) is not in that page's HTML as it is sent.
why: The page visitors use to decide (the order page, the contact page) leaves out the thing they came for, or shows it only after JavaScript runs, which search engines and assistants may not.
fix: Put the fact in the page's server-rendered HTML. A fact in an image's description only is not visible text: write it out.
tech: for each mustAppearOn path among the pages checked, the fact's declared value is in the visible text, a link or JSON-LD of the HTML as sent (image descriptions don't count, and say so)

title: Two of your feeds serve the same posts
what: Two feeds the page advertises list exactly the same item links.
why: Subscribers to one feed get the other's posts (a news feed serving the blog, say), and readers who follow both see everything twice.
fix: Point each feed at its own collection, usually a query or category filter that was copied from the other.
tech: The advertised feeds read for feed-broken (at most 3), compared as Sets of normalised item links: equal and non-empty, in any order. Sharing most items is not a duplicate

title: The feed this page advertises is not a feed
what: The advertised feed address answers, but with something that is not RSS or Atom, often an HTML page.
why: Feed readers cannot read it, so subscribers get nothing. A framework's catch-all route is the usual cause.
fix: Serve the feed's XML at that address, or point the link rel="alternate" tag at the address that does.
tech: the feed body does not start with an XML declaration, <rss> or <feed>

title: The feed this page advertises is too large
what: The feed response is larger than 2 MB.
why: Feed readers and aggregators time out or truncate large feeds, and frameworks such as Next.js do not cache responses over 2 MB, so every request rebuilds it.
fix: Limit the feed to recent items (20 to 50 is typical) and put a summary in each item instead of the full post.
tech: the feed response is larger than 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes)

title: The page still shows a prediction for something that already happened
what: A page lists a prediction, a pick or a preview whose event date is already past, and it does not show the result.
why: A prediction for a finished game or a past night looks careless at best, and misleads at worst: visitors act on it and the page loses their trust the next time.
fix: Remove the item or switch it to the result when the event ends. Generate the list from the schedule so an event leaves it by itself, and rebuild or revalidate the page after the result is in.
tech: for each rule with a forecast in gaugeline.freshness.json that is active, each item matching forecast.item (up to 200 per page) has its date read from forecast.date inside it, its own datetime or named attribute, or a time element with a datetime inside it, or the page's Event structured data with the property named in forecast.jsonld; the event is past when it is past at every instant the date could mean (a date alone is over when the whole day is, in the site's time zone; a time is over after forecast.lasts, 3h by default); an item that contains forecast.settled already shows its result and is skipped; no items, a date that cannot be read or an item with no date is could not check; the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page

title: A form now posts to a different address
what: A form still uses the same service, but posts to a different host than last run.
why: A different host can mean a different account or region with the same service, so entries may land where nobody reads them.
fix: Confirm the new address belongs to your account with that service.
tech: With --since last only: the same form key and provider, with a different action host

title: A language version doesn't link back
what: This page's hreflang points at a version in another language, but that version's hreflang doesn't point back.
why: Search engines ignore hreflang pairs that aren't confirmed from both sides, so searchers may get the wrong language.
fix: Give every version the same full set of hreflang links, including one to itself.
tech: page A has <link rel=alternate hreflang> to B, and B (fetched) has none to A (a trailing slash is not a difference)

title: Most of this page's HTML is a data payload
what: More than half of the HTML, and over 300 KB, is inline data (JSON, __NEXT_DATA__ or a framework's streamed payload) rather than content.
why: Every visitor downloads data the page may never show, and it delays the first paint on phones.
fix: Send only the fields the page renders. In Next.js, trim what getServerSideProps or a server component passes to client components.
tech: inline data scripts are over 300 KB (307,200 bytes) and more than half the HTML; not reported when html-huge is

title: Your calendar names a time zone it doesn't describe
what: Events in your .ics calendar use a TZID, but the file has no VTIMEZONE section for it.
why: The iCalendar standard requires the description. Some calendar apps fall back to UTC or the guest's zone without it, and show the wrong hour.
fix: Export the calendar with time zone definitions included, or add a VTIMEZONE for each TZID the events use.
tech: a DTSTART or DTEND TZID has no matching VTIMEZONE component (RFC 5545 §3.6.5)

title: Images are requested at an enormous width
what: An image is offered or requested 3840 pixels wide or more, wider than almost any screen shows it.
why: Phones and laptops may download a 4K-wide picture to show it a few hundred pixels across, which wastes data and slows the page.
fix: Cap the widths your image component generates (for Next.js, deviceSizes and imageSizes in next.config) and set the sizes attribute.
tech: a srcset candidate with a w descriptor, or a w= parameter, of 3840 or more

title: None of the images on this page are described
what: The page has images, and not one has alt text that says what it shows.
why: Screen reader users hear nothing about any picture, and search engines have no words to index the images by.
fix: Give each meaningful image an alt that says what it shows. alt="" is right for decorative images, but a page where every image is decorative is rare.
tech: every img has a missing, empty or whitespace-only alt

title: Some images are very large files
what: An image on the page is over 500 KB.
why: Large images are the most common reason a page is slow on a phone, and a slow page loses visitors before it loads.
fix: Resize the image to the size it is shown at and export it as WebP or AVIF, or serve it through an image CDN or your framework's image component.
tech: a sampled image's Content-Length header is over 512,000 bytes; a server that sends no Content-Length gives no finding

title: Images still load from an old WordPress site
what: Images on the page are served from /wp-content/uploads/, usually left over from a WordPress site the new site replaced.
why: When the old WordPress install or its host is switched off, every one of these images breaks at once.
fix: Move the images into the new site's own media library or asset folder and update the addresses.
tech: img src or srcset candidates under /wp-content/uploads/

title: A language version of this page is missing
what: The page says (through hreflang, the sitemap or your language settings) that it has a version in another language, but that version returns an error or redirects to the homepage.
why: Visitors who switch language land on an error or on the homepage, and search engines drop the alternate from results.
fix: Publish the missing version, or remove it from the page's hreflang links and the sitemap. Pages meant to exist in one language only can be excluded in gaugeline.languages.json.
tech: an expected twin (hreflang, sitemap xhtml:link or the configured prefix, subdomain or parameter) answers 4xx or 5xx, or redirects to / or a language root; at most 5 versions are fetched

title: Some links go through a link shortener
what: Links leave the page through a shortener or redirector (bit.ly, t.co, lnkd.in, a /redirect?url= address) instead of linking directly.
why: Visitors can't see where the link goes before they click, the redirect adds a delay, and if the shortener expires or is blocked the link breaks.
fix: Link straight to the destination. Social icons in the footer are a common place for these.
tech: a[href] on bit.ly, t.co, lnkd.in, buff.ly, ow.ly, tinyurl.com, goo.gl, rebrand.ly, is.gd, cutt.ly, shorturl.at, tiny.cc (or a subdomain), or a /redirect, /out or /go path with a url= style parameter holding an http(s) address; footer links count too

title: A listing shows a different address
what: The street number or ZIP code on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing is not the one on your site.
why: Maps sends people to the address on the listing. After a move, or with a typo, guests arrive at the wrong door.
fix: Correct the address in the listing's own dashboard, or on the site if the listing is the right one.
tech: the house number and the 5-digit ZIP code are read from both addresses and each one both sides state must be equal; street names are not compared; the site's address is the text fact "address" in gaugeline.facts.json, else the LocalBusiness address in structured data

title: A listing doesn't know about a holiday closure
what: Your site announces a day you are closed, such as Thanksgiving or Christmas, and a listing still shows its normal hours for that day.
why: People check the listing on the day. If it says you open at 4 on a day you are shut, they come anyway.
fix: Add the closure to the listing's special hours in its own dashboard (Google Business Profile: Special hours; Yelp for Business: Holiday hours).
tech: closures on the site are dates in LocalBusiness openingHoursSpecification (validFrom and validThrough, opens and closes both 00:00) and dates or fixed US holidays within 40 characters of the word "closed" in the pages read, from today in the venue's time zone up to 60 days ahead; a listing is missing one when its special hours (Google Business Profile, Yelp) do not mark that date closed; sources that give no special hours (Google Maps, Apple) are reported as could not check

title: Your llms.txt sends assistants to pages that don't work
what: Links in /llms.txt return an error (4xx or 5xx) or redirect to a different site.
why: llms.txt is a short guide for AI assistants to your most useful pages. A dead or off-site link is the page they quote, or fail to.
fix: Update the links to the pages' current addresses, or remove the ones that no longer exist.
tech: links in /llms.txt answer 4xx or 5xx, or redirect off-site

title: Your llms.txt gives assistants an old phone number, address or hours
what: The phone number, street address or opening hours in /llms.txt disagree with the page's structured data.
why: Assistants quote llms.txt directly. An old number or old hours there is what someone hears when they ask if you're open tonight.
fix: Update llms.txt to match the structured data (or the other way round, whichever is wrong). Generate both from one source if you can.
tech: hours, telephone or address in /llms.txt differ from the page's LocalBusiness JSON-LD

title: Some buttons open an email instead of a form
what: A contact button ("Talk to an expert", "Get a quote") opens one person's email program instead of a form.
why: The enquiry skips your CRM: it lands in one inbox with no campaign details, nobody else sees it, and visitors without an email program set up can't send it at all.
fix: Point the button at a form or a booking page that sends the enquiry to your CRM, and keep the email address as a plain fallback.
tech: a[href] starting mailto: with an address, whose text is a contact call to action (contact, talk, speak, get in touch, email us, book, quote, demo and similar) and not an address itself; one finding per page; the link's styling is not visible to Gaugeline

title: The menu changed since the last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, links in the header or footer menu were added, removed, moved to another parent, renamed or reordered.
why: A menu restructure changes many links at once and every page still loads, so nothing else reports the page that lost its only link.
fix: Check each change was meant. A removed link whose page now has no other link needs one, or a redirect if the page is gone.
tech: With --since last only. A link is its region, parent item and destination. Same destination under a new parent is moved; same identity with new text is renamed. A removed link whose destination has no inbound link from the pages read is high. On a first run (no saved menu yet): could not check

title: The footer isn't the same on every page
what: A page's footer links differ from the footer most of the pages read have, or a footer link gaugeline.nav.json marks as required (privacy, terms, contact) is missing.
why: A footer that differs on one template usually means that template was missed in a change; a missing privacy or terms link can be a legal problem.
fix: Use one footer for every template, and add any required link that is missing.
tech: With --since last or a gaugeline.nav.json (it reads the run's other pages). Footer destinations on the checked page and the run's other pages (4); the most common set is the reference. Required links match a footer link's text or path, case-insensitively

title: Menu items go to the homepage
what: Links in the menu or header point at the homepage but are labelled as something else, such as Services or Contact.
why: Visitors who click Services land back on the homepage and think the page is missing. It usually means a menu item was added with no link.
fix: Point each menu item at its own page, or remove it until the page exists.
tech: a nav or header a[href] resolving to / whose text (or aria-label) is not Home or the site's name

title: Pages in the sitemap that no page links to
what: Addresses the sitemap lists that none of the pages read link to, in their menus, footers or text.
why: Visitors can only reach them from search or an old bookmark, and search engines treat a page nothing links to as unimportant.
fix: Link to each page from its section's menu or a related page, or take it out of the sitemap if it is gone.
tech: With --since last or a gaugeline.nav.json (it reads the run's other pages). Same-site sitemap addresses (one level of index) against every link on the checked page and the run's other pages (4); the checked page itself is excepted. A page linked only from a page not read is reported too: the evidence says how many were read

title: The mobile menu is missing links the desktop menu has
what: The page has a separate mobile menu, and some destinations in the desktop header menu aren't in it.
why: Most visitors are on a phone: a page missing from the mobile menu is missing for them.
fix: Add the missing links to the mobile menu, or build both menus from one list.
tech: The separate mobile menu's destinations (gaugeline.nav.json regions.mobile, or a [data-mobile-menu], #mobile-menu or .mobile-menu element) against the header's. A menu toggle whose menu isn't in the HTML is could not check: it is built at a phone width, which needs a rendered read (not on yet)

title: The page still shows an old copy after an edit
what: With a content source connected, this Next.js page is still a cached copy made before its document last changed, more than 10 minutes after the change.
why: Editors publish a fix and visitors keep seeing the old version, so the fix looks broken.
fix: Revalidate the page when its document changes (an on-demand revalidation webhook from the CMS), or lower its revalidate time.
tech: Next.js sites with a content source (branch 30) only, otherwise unchecked: x-nextjs-cache or x-vercel-cache HIT or STALE with an Age header, the copy's age older than the document's last change, and the change more than 10 minutes ago. Without an Age header nothing is reported

title: The share picture doesn't load
what: The og:image the page names answers with an error, or can't be reached.
why: When someone shares the page, the preview card shows no picture, or none at all, on the day you most want it to look right.
fix: Point og:image at an image that loads on the live domain (open the address in a browser to check), and use a full https:// address.
tech: One probe of the og:image address (HEAD, then GET on 405/501), counted in the images budget; 4xx, 5xx or no answer is a finding. No og:image is og-image-missing's to report

title: Shared links may show no picture
what: og:image is a relative address (like /previews/landing.webp), not a full https:// address.
why: Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack and iMessage need a full address. With a relative one, shares of the page show no picture.
fix: Write og:image as a full address, including https:// and the domain. Most frameworks have a site URL setting for this.
tech: og:image does not start with http:// or https:// (protocol-relative // addresses are flagged too)

title: Shared links point at a different page than search engines see
what: The page's og:url (the address social apps use when it is shared) differs from its canonical tag.
why: Likes and shares are counted against one address while search engines rank another, and a share can open the wrong page.
fix: Set og:url to the same address as the canonical tag. Both usually come from one SEO component.
tech: og:url and <link rel="canonical"> differ by scheme, host, path or query (a trailing slash is not a difference)

title: This page is heavy to load
what: The HTML plus the images Gaugeline sampled add up to over 3 MB, and that is a floor: unsampled files come on top.
why: On a phone connection a page this heavy takes many seconds and costs visitors data.
fix: Start with the largest files in the evidence: resize and compress images, and trim the HTML's inline data.
tech: HTML bytes plus the Content-Length of sampled images (the files the run already requested) is over 3 MB (3,145,728 bytes); no extra requests are made

title: A listing has fewer items than last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, a repeated list on a page (products, posts, people, events) has fewer items, with the ones that are gone where items carry links.
why: A shop page with 7 products instead of 12 still looks complete: items drop out when a feed, a filter or a category breaks, and nobody counts.
fix: Check the items that are gone were removed on purpose. If they weren't, look at what feeds the list. A listing meant to shrink goes under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json.
tech: With --since last only. A list is a ul or ol with 3 or more items, or an element marked data-list, in the main content; it is named by its data-list value or the heading before it. For a paginated list only the first page is compared, and the evidence says so. On a first run: could not check

title: A page lost its structured data since the last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, a structured-data type that a page had (Product, Recipe, Event, Article) is no longer there.
why: Search results show rich listings (prices, ratings, dates) only from structured data; when a template or plugin change drops it, the page reads the same and the listing quietly goes plain.
fix: Put the markup back where the template lost it, or list the page under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json when it was removed on purpose.
tech: With --since last only. Types are read from JSON-LD @type and microdata itemtype, with the schema.org prefix dropped. One finding per page, naming every type gone. On a first run: could not check

title: The site shows two different handles for one payment service
what: With no payment details set, the pages checked show two or more different handles for the same service.
why: At most one of them is right. Customers can't tell which, and some pay the other one.
fix: Keep the right handle everywhere, and set it in gaugeline.payments.json so Gaugeline checks against it.
tech: Only without gaugeline.payments.json: a Zelle, Cash App, Venmo or PayPal handle with more than one distinct value (compared case-insensitively; Zelle phones by digits) across the pages checked

title: The page shows placeholder images
what: Images on the page come from a placeholder service such as placehold.co, dummyimage.com or picsum.photos.
why: Visitors see grey boxes or random stock photos where the real product or team picture should be.
fix: Upload the real images and point the img tags at them.
tech: img src on placehold.co, placehold.it, placeholder.com, via.placeholder.com, dummyimage.com, picsum.photos, placekitten.com, placebear.com, loremflickr.com, fakeimg.pl, placeimg.com, lorempixel.com (or a subdomain)

title: The page still has placeholder text
what: The page shows unfinished copy: lorem ipsum, TODO or TBD, a [bracketed placeholder], or a title or main heading such as Untitled, Staging or Test.
why: Visitors see an unfinished site, and search engines may show the placeholder in results.
fix: Replace the placeholder with the real copy. Search the CMS for "lorem", "TODO" and "[" before publishing.
tech: main content text matches "lorem ipsum", TODO/TBD/FIXME or [insert ...]-style brackets (code and pre ignored), or the whole title or h1 is one of "untitled", "untitled page", "untitled document", "new page", "page title", "title", "test", "test page", "testing", "staging", "staging site", "my site", "my website", "site title", "home page title" (English lists)

title: Your address takes several jumps to load
what: The address you entered redirects more than once before the page loads.
why: Each jump slows the first visit and can weaken how search engines credit the page.
fix: Point every redirect straight at the final address.
tech: more than one 3xx hop on the entered URL

title: A breadcrumb ends on a different page
what: The last item of a page's breadcrumb structured data points at an address other than the page's own canonical.
why: The trail should end where the visitor is. One that ends elsewhere usually means the breadcrumb was copied from another page.
fix: Make the last ListItem's item the page's canonical address, or leave the last item's URL out.
tech: the highest-position ListItem has a URL that differs from the canonical (or the page address) by scheme, host, path or query; needs a gaugeline.schema.json

title: Structured data refers to something that isn't there
what: A structured data reference ({"@id": ...}) points at a node that is not defined on the page or on the other pages checked.
why: Search engines can't follow the reference, so whatever it stands for (the publisher, the author, the organization) is lost.
fix: Define the node the reference names (usually on the homepage), or correct the @id to the one you use.
tech: an object with only an @id resolves (after normalisation) to no @id defined on the sampled pages

title: Pages redefine your organization instead of referring to it
what: Pages other than the homepage define the Organization or WebSite again, with its properties, instead of referring to the one node by its @id as your schema guide says.
why: Copies drift: one page gets an old logo or phone number, and search engines see several organizations where there should be one.
fix: On every other page, write {"@id": "<the configured id>"} where the Organization or WebSite is needed, and define it once on the homepage.
tech: an Organization or WebSite node with properties beyond @id and @type on a page other than / (needs organizationId or websiteId in gaugeline.schema.json)

title: A page is missing structured data its template requires
what: A page that matches one of your schema guide's templates (for example /blog/*) lacks a type the guide requires there, such as Article or BreadcrumbList.
why: Rich results for that kind of page depend on the type, and one template that drifted usually means every page built from it did.
fix: Add the missing type to the template's structured data component.
tech: the most specific matching template's require list has a type missing from the page's JSON-LD (@type anywhere, @graph included); common subtypes count (an AboutPage is a WebPage, a BlogPosting an Article); needs templates in gaugeline.schema.json

title: Your sitemap lists pages on a different address
what: Every entry in the sitemap uses a different host than the site, for example a staging domain or the other of www and the bare domain.
why: Search engines ignore sitemap entries for a host the sitemap does not belong to, so the sitemap does nothing for this site.
fix: Generate the sitemap with the site's public address. In most frameworks this is a site URL or base URL setting.
tech: every sitemap entry's host differs from the page's host

title: Search engines can't find a list of your pages
what: There is no sitemap at /sitemap.xml, and robots.txt does not say where one is.
why: Without a sitemap, search engines find pages only by following links, so new or deep pages take longer to appear.
fix: Publish a sitemap at /sitemap.xml (most site builders and frameworks can generate one) and add a Sitemap: line with its full address to robots.txt.
tech: /sitemap.xml is not a 200 sitemap and robots.txt has no Sitemap: line

title: Your sitemap lists old addresses that redirect
what: Pages listed in the sitemap answer with a redirect (3xx) instead of the page.
why: A sitemap should list the final address of each page. Redirecting entries make search engines do extra work and can keep the old address in results.
fix: List each page at the address it redirects to. This often follows a move to https, to www, or to a new URL scheme.
tech: sampled sitemap entries return 3xx

title: The same structured data is on this page twice
what: A schema.org type is described both in JSON-LD and as microdata (itemtype) on the same page.
why: Search engines see two descriptions of one thing, which can disagree, and may pick the wrong one or ignore both.
fix: Keep one: usually the JSON-LD, and remove the itemscope and itemtype attributes from the theme or plugin that adds microdata.
tech: a schema.org @type in JSON-LD is also a microdata itemtype

title: A page does not say what it should for the current switch
what: You said what a page must tell visitors while a feature is on or off ("order at the bar" while pre-orders are off), and the page does not say it.
why: A visitor who reaches the page learns nothing: no explanation, no other way to order. They are left guessing whether the site is broken.
fix: Show the message from the same switch that turns the feature off, so the two cannot disagree. If the evidence says a cache served the page, purge it after the switch changes.
tech: for each switch in gaugeline.switches.json, the page text for the current state (whenOff.pageSays while off, whenOn.pageSays while on) is read from the page as sent, without JavaScript, with hidden elements left out; the phrase is matched case-insensitively and ignoring accents, spacing and punctuation, in the page's own language when the phrase is given per language (a bilingual site's other-language pages are read through gaugeline.languages.json); a page that answers 404, a source or a page that cannot be read is could not check (the link checks report dead pages); the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page

title: A tracking rule points at something that no longer exists
what: A Tag Manager trigger waits for a page address, link, form or element that no page on the site has, so its tags never fire.
why: Tag rules outlive the pages they were written for: a download or form trigger tied to a retired address goes quiet, and the report just shows fewer leads.
fix: Point the trigger at what the site uses now (the nearest match is in the evidence), or delete it and the tags that only it fires.
tech: The container export named in gaugeline.tags.json (no Tag Manager account is used). Page address conditions are compared with the pages read, their same-site links and the sitemap; click and form conditions (Click URL, ID, Classes, Text, Element; Form ID, Classes, Text, URL, Element) with the elements of the pages read. A trigger type, variable or comparison it doesn't read, a custom event, or a trigger limited to pages the run didn't read is listed under could not check

title: Two tags send the same event at the same moment
what: Two Tag Manager tags that aren't paused send the same event to the same place on the same trigger.
why: Every lead, download or sale is counted twice, so conversion numbers and the ad bidding built on them are wrong.
fix: Keep one of the tags and pause or delete the other (usually the copy).
tech: The container export named in gaugeline.tags.json, read without requests. GA4 event tags are the same when the event name and the measurement ID match; any other tag type when its type and every setting match. Paused tags are left out

title: This page isn't set up for phone screens
what: The page has no viewport meta tag, so phones show it zoomed out as if on a desktop screen.
why: Visitors have to pinch and zoom to read anything, and Google treats the page as not mobile-friendly.
fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the page's head.
tech: no <meta name="viewport"> anywhere in the document

title: A title tag isn't what the plan says
what: The title tag the preview sends isn't the one the plan gives the page.
why: Someone edited the page, or the template overrode it, and the title the plan chose for search is gone.
fix: Set the page's title to the plan's, or update the plan if the change was deliberate.
tech: The page row's Title Tag against the HTML title, compared trimmed, case-folded, whitespace collapsed, quotes and dashes straightened; a brand suffix counts. No title in the HTML is reported with a hint that it may be set by JavaScript

title: An H1 isn't what the plan says
what: The page's first H1 isn't the one the plan gives it.
why: Usually a content change nobody recorded; the heading the plan chose for the keyword is gone.
fix: Set the H1 to the plan's, or update the plan.
tech: The page row's H1 against the first h1 in the HTML, compared like titles; a page with several H1s is noted

title: A planned #section isn't on the page
what: A plan row with a #section points at an id that isn't on the page.
why: Links to the section land at the top of the page, and the plan's section was never built.
fix: Add the section with that id, or change the row to the id the page uses.
tech: The row's fragment against every element id in the HTML the preview sends

title: An old address takes more than one redirect
what: An old address takes two or more redirects to reach its page.
why: Each hop costs visitors time, and search engines follow only so many before giving up on passing signals.
fix: Redirect the old address straight to the final page. A server that adds a trailing slash first counts: redirect the old address's own form.
tech: More than one 3xx in the hop list the fetcher records; the trail is in the evidence

title: A menu item and its page are named differently
what: A menu item matches no page by name, and exactly one page shares a distinctive word with it.
why: The menu and the page plan disagree on the name, so the page's title, H1 and keyword may not be what visitors click.
fix: Use one name in both places, or record the difference on purpose.
tech: Distinctive words are five letters or more, not health, healthcare, medical, service(s) or management. Exactly one page name with one of them; the evidence gives both labels and both lines

title: A menu item links to a page that still needs building
what: A menu item matches a page row whose Status says Need Page.
why: The menu will link to a page that hasn't been built: at launch it is a 404 in the navigation.
fix: Build the page before launch, or leave the item out of the menu until it exists.
tech: The matched row's Status cell against /need(s) page/i. Skipped, with a note, when the plan has no Status column

title: Two rows in the plan have the same title tag
what: Two or more rows of the plan plan the same title tag.
why: Search engines show the title in results; two pages with one title compete with each other and neither looks like the answer.
fix: Write a title that says what is different about each page.
tech: Title Tag cells compared trimmed, whitespace collapsed, lower case, with curly quotes and dashes straightened; a brand suffix is part of the title. Empty cells are left out

title: Two rows in the plan have the same H1
what: Two or more rows of the plan plan the same H1.
why: The H1 tells visitors and search engines what the page is about; two pages with the same heading read as the same page.
fix: Give each page a heading that names its own topic.
tech: H1 cells compared the same way as titles. Empty cells are left out

title: A slug misspells its own heading
what: A word in a page's address is one or two letters away from a word in the same row's page name or H1, such as credentialling for Credentialing.
why: The address is permanent once it is indexed and linked; fixing a typo later means a redirect, and until then the page looks careless in results.
fix: Use the heading's spelling in the slug (the corrected path is in the evidence) before the page is built.
tech: Words of 5+ letters in the last path segment, not in the row's page name or H1, within Damerau distance 1 of a heading word (2 for words of 8+ letters). Plural and tense endings (s, es, ed, ing) and listed British/American pairs are excused; accents are folded. One finding per row

title: Two pages in the plan target the same primary keyword
what: Two or more pages of the plan have the same Primary Keyword, so they will compete for one search before a line of code is written.
why: Search engines show one page per query from a site; two pages chasing the same term split their links and usually both rank worse than one would.
fix: Give each page its own primary keyword, or merge the pages into one.
tech: Primary Keyword cells compared trimmed, lower case, spaces collapsed, quotes straightened and a trailing full stop removed; no stemming (singular and plural differ). Empty, n/a, none, tbd, - and bracketed placeholders are left out. A page and its anchor rows count once. Groups sorted by a Primary Volume column when there is one

title: Some old addresses in the plan's notes aren't settled
what: A notes column read with --legacy-from mentions a legacy page in words instead of by its address, or asks whether it should redirect, so no redirect can be checked for it.
why: Old addresses that rank keep their traffic only with a 301 to the right new page. A note nobody resolved is a redirect nobody will build.
fix: Put the old address in the note ("301 legacy /old-page here.") or decide and write it, then run the plan check again.
tech: Sentences in the --legacy-from columns containing "legacy": one that says 301 but names no path (no-path), or one with a path that starts with Confirm, contains whether or ends with a question mark (unconfirmed). One finding listing every line

title: A printed link to a page now lands on the home page
what: A printed link to a page deeper than the home page now lands on the home page.
why: The classic lazy redirect after a restructure: the visitor who scanned for the menu has to find it again.
fix: Redirect the printed address to the page that replaced the one it was printed for, and add its expectedDestination to the register.
tech: No expectedDestination; the printed path isn't / and the trail ends on /

title: A printed address loses its tracking tags
what: A printed address's utm_ (or other configured) parameters are gone by the time it reaches its page.
why: Scans of that table tent or flyer can't be counted: the campaign looks like it did nothing.
fix: Pass the query string on in the redirect.
tech: Parameters on the printed URL whose names start with a tag prefix (utm_ by default) and are missing from the final address

title: The same product is in Printful more than once
what: Two or more Printful products have the same name, or the same external id.
why: An order for the product can be made from either copy, with different designs or prices, and the shop only knows one of them.
fix: Keep one product, delete the rest in Printful and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: Printful store products grouped by normaliseName, then by external id (trimmed, exact), each in one pass into a Map; a product in a name group and an external id group is listed once, in the name group; one finding per group with every copy's id, up to 10 and then a count; a blank external id or a name that normalises to nothing is never a group; runs only when Printful returned data

title: The same product is on the website more than once
what: Two or more published Sanity products have the same name, or the same non-empty SKU.
why: The shop has the same product twice, so a price, a photo or a stock figure can be right on one copy and wrong on the other, and a link to checkout may be saved on only one of them.
fix: Keep one product, unpublish or delete the rest in Sanity and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: published Sanity products grouped by normaliseName, then by SKU (trimmed, lower-case), each in one pass into a Map; a product in a name group and a SKU group is listed once, in the name group; one finding per group with every copy's _id, up to 10 and then a count; an empty SKU or a name that normalises to nothing is never a group; runs only when Sanity returned data

title: The same product is in Stripe more than once
what: Two or more active Stripe products have the same name once case, spacing and punctuation are ignored.
why: Until one record is the real one, nothing can say what checkout should charge: the copies may carry different prices, and the website may point at any of them.
fix: Keep one, archive the rest in Stripe and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: active Stripe products grouped by normaliseName in one pass into a Map; one finding per group listing every copy with its id and default price, up to 10 and then a count; archived products are not counted as copies and are named in the finding when their group also has active ones; names that normalise to an empty string are never grouped; runs only when Stripe returned data

title: Fulfillment lists a different price
what: A synced Printful variant's retail price is different from the price Stripe charges for the product.
why: Anything that reads Printful's price (a storefront sync, an invoice, a packing slip) shows customers a different number from the one they paid.
fix: Decide which price you mean, then change the other so the two agree, or have Printful's retail price follow checkout.
tech: each synced sync_variants.retail_price of the matched Printful product against the unit_amount of the matched Stripe product's default price, both whole minor units; compared only when the variant's currency is known and equal to Stripe's (a different currency is a notice, never converted); a variant with no retail price, or a Stripe default price with no fixed amount, is skipped with a notice; one finding per product listing up to three differing variants and both match rules

title: No default price in checkout
what: An active Stripe product that is matched to a product on your website has no default price.
why: Anything that asks Stripe for the product's price (a payment link, a checkout session, a price comparison) finds nothing, and the product cannot be bought or compared.
fix: In Stripe, open the product and set one of its prices as the default, or archive the product if it is no longer sold.
tech: a matched Stripe product with active true and default_price null, whether or not it has other prices; the evidence says how many prices it has; archived products and Stripe products with no Sanity partner are not reported

title: A plan's free trial differs from checkout
what: The page promises a free trial that the matched Stripe price does not give, or Stripe gives a trial the page never mentions.
why: Someone who signs up for a free trial and is charged today, or who is surprised by a trial that hides when the first bill comes, files a dispute.
fix: Make the page and the Stripe price agree on the trial's length, or take the promise off the page.
tech: a trial of N days, weeks or months written next to the plan's name (7-day free trial, prueba gratis de 7 dias) against recurring.trial_period_days of the matched price (a month is 28 to 31 days); a trial set when checkout is created (subscription_data) is not visible on the price, so confirm there before changing the page

title: A query does not leave drafts out
what: The filter of a query in your code does not leave drafts out.
why: With the published perspective in the client that is safe. If anything runs the query with drafts included (preview mode, a token with the wrong perspective), unpublished content reaches a visitor.
fix: Add !(_id in path("drafts.**")) to the filter, or make sure the client always asks for the published perspective. Gaugeline cannot see the client, only the query.
tech: read from the repository with no request: the query's filter is parsed and does not require !(_id in path("drafts.**")) (or match "drafts.*") in an && chain

title: Two documents share a title
what: Two or more published documents of one type are called the same thing, ignoring case and spaces around the title.
why: Different addresses, same name: usually content that was duplicated and not moved, which splits search results between two pages. It can also be two real pages that need different names.
fix: Open the documents named by their ids. If one is a copy, delete it and redirect its address; if both are real, rename one so a visitor can tell them apart.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never read), projecting only _id, "slug": slug.current and title; one pass puts each id into a Map from the slug as it is, or from the trimmed and lower-cased title, to the ids that have it, and a bucket with more than one id is a group; documents with no slug or no title are left out of that key, a draft id is skipped, and types are grouped apart; a title shared by two or more ids of one type that do not all share one slug

title: A webhook endpoint is switched off
what: A Stripe webhook endpoint has the status disabled.
why: Stripe sends a disabled endpoint nothing. If your site still depends on it, payments are made and the site is not told.
fix: If the endpoint is still needed, enable it in the Stripe dashboard (Stripe may have disabled it after days of failures, so read its last attempts first). If it is not, delete it so the list says what is live.
tech: GET /v1/webhook_endpoints; an endpoint whose status is disabled is a finding, whatever it takes; the evidence is the endpoint's host only

title: The certificate no longer covers a name it did
what: The https certificate after cutover lacks a name the one before covered (www, a subdomain), or there is no certificate where there was one.
why: Visitors on the name that dropped off see a security warning instead of the site.
fix: Add the missing name to the new host's certificate (most hosts add www as a separate domain).
tech: Names from subjectAltName, a wildcard covering one label. A new issuer or a renewed date alone is not a change

title: The domain's DNS records changed at cutover
what: Against the snapshot taken before cutover, the domain's DMARC record, a DKIM key (for the selectors in gaugeline.cutover.json) or its address records (A, AAAA) are different.
why: A lost DKIM key or DMARC record breaks mail authentication quietly; new address records are the cutover itself, worth confirming they point where the new host says.
fix: Check each value against what the new host and your mail provider publish. List a change that was meant under expectedChanges in gaugeline.cutover.json.
tech: TXT at _dmarc.<domain> (v=DMARC1), TXT at <selector>._domainkey.<domain>, A and AAAA at the domain; sets compared. A lookup that failed in either run is could not check

title: Some AI assistants can't read your site
what: robots.txt stops one or more known AI crawlers from reading the home page. Gaugeline says which, and whether the block names them or comes from a rule for every crawler.
why: People ask assistants about a business before they open its site. Blocking AI crawlers is a fair choice; blocking them by accident means assistants answer from old or second-hand information.
fix: If the block is on purpose, there is nothing to do. If it comes from a Disallow: / meant for a staging site, remove it, or add groups for the assistants you want to allow.
tech: known AI user-agent tokens (packages/core/src/data/ai-agents.json) are disallowed / by robots.txt

title: The store lists the app under a different name
what: The name the App Store or Google Play shows for a linked app differs from the name you expect.
why: A renamed or replaced app can mean the link points at an old listing, or at someone else's app.
fix: Check the link points at the right listing. If the app was renamed on purpose, update the expected name.
tech: the store's app name differs from the expected app name (case, punctuation and a leading "The" ignored); only runs when an expected name is set

title: A downloadable file is on a public asset address
what: A page links to a file (pdf, zip, epub, mp3, mp4, docx or xlsx) on a public asset store and shows no price, or the link is a terms, privacy or policy page.
why: That is fine for a brochure or a menu. It becomes a problem the day the file is something a customer bought, because anyone with the address can open it.
fix: If the file is free, nothing to do. If it will ever be sold, serve it from a download route that checks the purchase and hands back a short-lived signed link.
tech: a[href] to a file with a sold file type on a public asset store host, on a page with no price, or whose link text is terms, privacy or policy; one finding per page; the file is never requested; the query string is not printed; a signed address with an expiry is a pass

title: The site wouldn't let Gaugeline read the page
what: The page answered with a refusal (401, 403, 429, 503 with Retry-After) or a bot-challenge page instead of its content.
why: A firewall or bot protection is in front of the site. That isn't a broken site, but it can also stop search engines' and AI assistants' crawlers, and nothing else could be checked.
fix: If the site should be readable by crawlers, allow them in the firewall or bot-protection settings. Gaugeline never retries or disguises itself to get through.
tech: The final answer for the page is 401, 403, 429, 503 with a Retry-After header, or a 200 under 60 words with a known challenge marker (Just a moment, Attention Required, cf-chl, a captcha form). Every check that needs the page is then listed as could not check; only robots.txt and DNS checks run

title: The page doesn't say which address is the real one
what: There's no canonical tag.
why: Copies of the page with tracking parameters can be treated as separate pages.
fix: Add a self-referencing canonical tag.
tech: no <link rel="canonical">

title: A page of changing numbers does not say when they were updated
what: A page under one of your freshness rules shows no update time at all, in the place you named or in its structured data.
why: Without a stamp nobody can tell fresh numbers from stale ones, and neither can Gaugeline: a sync can stop and the page gives no sign.
fix: Print the time the data was last updated on the page, from the same record the numbers come from (a time element with a datetime attribute, or dateModified in the structured data), then point the rule at it.
tech: for each rule with a stamp in gaugeline.freshness.json that is active (in the months of activeWhen, in the site's time zone), the page as sent without JavaScript has no element matching the selector with a datetime, content, named attribute or text, and no property of that name in its structured data; a stamp that is there but cannot be read is not reported here (data-stale lists it as could not check); a rule that is not active is listed as could not check, not passed

title: Your Sanity content can be read by anyone
what: The Sanity dataset your images come from answers queries without a token.
why: That is fine for a blog, and a risk the day someone adds a form or an order type to it: everything in it is readable by anyone who looks.
fix: If nothing in it is private, nothing to do. Otherwise make the dataset private in sanity.io/manage and give the site a read token.
tech: Project and dataset read from cdn.sanity.io image addresses; one GET to <project>.api.sanity.io with the query {"count": count(*), "types": array::unique(*[]._type)} and no token, at most 2 datasets; never document contents

title: Your DMARC policy only watches
what: The domain's DMARC record has p=none: receiving servers report mail that fails, and deliver it anyway.
why: That is the right first step, and it doesn't stop anyone sending mail as you. Left at none, it never will.
fix: Read the DMARC reports for a few weeks, fix any service of yours that fails, then change p=none to p=quarantine (and later p=reject).
tech: Public DNS only: the TXT record at _dmarc.<host> starting v=DMARC1 has p=none; sp (the subdomain policy) does not change this

title: Some events are missing details search engines need
what: An event in the page's structured data has no start date, no location or no event status.
why: Google needs these to show the event in results, and the status is how a cancelled or moved night is shown as such.
fix: Give every Event a startDate, a location and an eventStatus (for example https://schema.org/EventScheduled).
tech: Event JSON-LD without startDate, location or eventStatus (one finding listing each event and what it lacks)

title: Two menu links report the same click
what: Two links to the same page, under different parent menus, send identical event values, so the report can't tell which one was clicked.
why: A comparison of a new menu is only real if every link reports where it sits: identical values merge the two links into one row.
fix: Add the parent menu (or another value that tells them apart) to the event both links send.
tech: Links that passed events-fire, grouped by destination: two with different parent menus whose events carry the same values for the plan's parameters. Needs a rendered read (G39): until then it is could not check

title: Several form services on one page
what: Forms or form scripts from more than one service (for example HubSpot and Typeform) are on the same page.
why: Leads from one page end up in different places, and each service needs its own tracking, consent and follow-up.
fix: Check that each form is meant to be there, and move the page to one service if you can.
tech: Sightings of more than one of Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot, Formstack, Marketo and Typeform on one page (form action, iframe src, embed script); the tracking code alone is not a sighting

title: A hidden section is past its launch date
what: Today is after the launch date set for a hidden section, and gaugeline.hidden.json still lists it as hidden.
why: Either the launch slipped and nobody updated the plan, or it launched and the hidden checks are now guarding the wrong thing.
fix: Move the until date, or remove the section from gaugeline.hidden.json now that it's live.
tech: A hidden section's until date (YYYY-MM-DD, the whole day in UTC) is before the run's clock; no request is made

title: Some language codes are not valid
what: hreflang uses a code that isn't a valid language tag (such as "sp" or "es_US"), or a page with three or more languages has no x-default.
why: Search engines ignore an hreflang with an invalid code, and without x-default they guess which version to show everyone else.
fix: Use BCP 47 codes such as es, es-US or es-419 (a hyphen, not an underscore), and add hreflang="x-default" for the version to show when no language matches.
tech: an hreflang value is not a BCP 47 tag (two-letter languages must be ISO 639-1), or 3+ distinct languages have no x-default

title: Some images have no alt attribute
what: Some images have no alt attribute at all, not even an empty one.
why: Without alt, screen readers read the file name aloud. An empty alt="" tells them to skip a decorative image; a missing one does not.
fix: Add alt to every img: a short description, or alt="" for decorative images.
tech: img elements with no alt attribute (one finding with a count and the first three)

title: Images use older, heavier file formats
what: Images are served as JPEG, PNG or GIF with no WebP or AVIF version offered.
why: WebP and AVIF are usually a quarter to a half smaller for the same picture, so the page loads faster.
fix: Offer WebP or AVIF with a <picture> element or srcset, or let your image CDN or framework image component pick the format.
tech: a sampled image's Content-Type is image/jpeg, image/png or image/gif and it has no WebP or AVIF candidate (SVG is never reported)

title: A language version declares the wrong language
what: A version's <html lang> names a different language than the version is (for example the Spanish page still says lang="en").
why: Screen readers read the page with the wrong voice and pronunciation, and browsers offer to translate it into its own language.
fix: Set <html lang> per version from the page's language, usually in the layout component.
tech: <html lang>'s primary subtag differs from the version's language (from hreflang or the configured scheme)

title: Some text wasn't translated
what: Strings you listed as default-language text (button labels, headings) appear on another language version.
why: A Spanish page with an English "Add to cart" button looks unfinished, and some visitors won't know what it does.
fix: Translate the strings in the components that render them; they are usually hard-coded in a shared button or heading.
tech: a string from untranslated in gaugeline.languages.json appears in another version's main text or link names (case ignored); needs the list

title: Some links don't say where they go
what: Links whose whole text is "read more", "click here", "learn more" or "here".
why: Screen reader users often browse a page by its links, and hear a list of identical "read more"s. Search engines also read link text to understand the destination.
fix: Make the link text name the destination, such as "Read more about pricing", or add an aria-label that does.
tech: a link's accessible name (aria-label, else its text) is exactly "read more", "click here", "learn more", "here" (English list)

title: Links on this page go through a redirect
what: Links to other pages on the site answer with a redirect (3xx) before reaching the page.
why: Each redirect adds a round trip for visitors, and search engines pass a little less on through every hop.
fix: Change the link to the address it ends up at. This usually follows a move to new URLs, https or www.
tech: a sampled same-site a[href] answers 3xx first and ends in 200

title: One page has two names in your menus
what: The same link appears in the menu, header or footer with two different labels.
why: Visitors wonder whether the two labels are two pages, and the site reads as unfinished.
fix: Use one label for each page everywhere. Menus kept in two places (a header and a footer component) drift apart first.
tech: one href (a #fragment makes a different destination) has more than one distinct label across nav, header and footer (case and trailing arrows ignored)

title: Shared links have no picture
what: The page has no og:image tag.
why: When the page is shared in a chat or a social post, it shows as a plain link with no picture, which fewer people click.
fix: Add <meta property="og:image" content="https://..."> with a 1200 by 630 picture for the page.
tech: no og:image (or og:image:url) meta property

title: A price changed since the last run
what: A product's price in the page's structured data is different from the last run's.
why: Sometimes that is the plan. When it isn't (a sync from the shop, an edit to the wrong product), customers and search results see the wrong price.
fix: If the change wasn't meant, correct the price at its source (the shop or CMS) and rebuild; if it was, nothing to do.
tech: With --since last only: the JSON-LD Offer price (integer minor units; anything but 48 or 48.00 is unread) for a product key (sku or name plus currency) present in both runs

title: Breadcrumbs don't start where your guide says
what: The first item of a page's breadcrumb structured data is not the Home name and address your schema guide sets.
why: Search results show the breadcrumb trail; one that starts somewhere else on some pages looks inconsistent and can point at the wrong page.
fix: Start every BreadcrumbList with the configured first item, for example Home at /.
tech: the lowest-position ListItem's name or URL differs from breadcrumbs.firstName / breadcrumbs.firstUrl in gaugeline.schema.json (name case ignored, URL resolved)

title: A phone link may not dial correctly
what: A tel: link has spaces or brackets in the number.
why: Some phones and click-to-call tools dial the wrong number, or nothing, when the link has spaces or brackets.
fix: Write the link as digits with a leading + and country code, for example href="tel:+14155550100". Keep the spaced format in the visible text only.
tech: an a[href^="tel:"] contains a space, ( or ); "-" and "." pass. One finding per distinct number

title: A temporary address doesn't name the real one
what: The page is served from a hosting provider's temporary address and has no canonical tag.
why: If a search engine finds the temporary address, nothing tells it the real page is on your domain, and the preview can show up in results.
fix: Add <link rel="canonical" href="https://yourdomain/..."> to every page, so each preview points at the real address.
tech: The final address's host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev and the HTML has no link rel=canonical

title: Invisible characters sit inside words on the page
what: Zero-width characters are inside words in the page's visible text.
why: A word with a hidden character in it no longer matches itself: search can't find it, and copy-pasted or tampered text can carry marks nobody meant to publish.
fix: Remove them from the source text: retype the word, or paste it as plain text.
tech: U+200B to U+200D, U+2060 to U+2064, U+180E or U+FEFF between two Latin, Cyrillic, Greek or digit characters in visible text; emoji joiners, Persian non-joiners and zero-width marks at the end of a text (content source maps) are not counted

title: A redirect drops the old address's query string
what: An old address with a query string redirects to an address without it.
why: Campaign tags and filters on old links are lost, so their visits can't be told apart.
fix: Pass the query string on in the redirect rule.
tech: The legacy address has a query; the trail's final address has none

title: Addresses in the rank export are neither live nor planned
what: Pages in the --rank export (Search Console or a rank tracker) are neither in the --live list nor in the plan.
why: Usually the export is of another site or property, or of pages already gone: the numbers on the uncovered list may not be the site's.
fix: Check the export is of this site's property and recent, or add the pages to --live if they still exist.
tech: Export paths (the --live key: lower case, no trailing slash, no query or host) not in the set of live paths or row paths. One finding with the count and three examples

title: One page's primary keyword is another page's secondary
what: A page's Primary Keyword is also listed as a Secondary Keyword of other pages.
why: Often deliberate, supporting pages in a cluster; worth a look, because a strong supporting page can outrank the page meant to win the term.
fix: Check the supporting pages link to the primary page, and that none of them is built to rank for the term itself.
tech: Each Secondary Keyword cell is split on commas, semicolons and line breaks and compared like primaries. Reported from the primary's side, only when one page has the term as its primary

title: A printed address takes more than two redirects
what: A printed address takes more than two redirects to land.
why: Every hop is a wait on a phone, often on a weak signal, and one broken hop breaks the code.
fix: Redirect the printed address straight to its page.
tech: More than two 3xx in the trail; the trail is in the evidence

title: On the website, not in fulfillment
what: A product on your website has no matching product in Printful.
why: For something you print, nobody will make the order. For a ticket, a download or a service, that is expected and nothing needs fixing.
fix: If the product should be printed, create it in Printful or save its Printful id on the website product. Otherwise leave it.
tech: a published Sanity product that matchProducts paired with no Printful product; runs only when both Sanity and Printful returned data; low because most shops sell some products that are not printed; one finding per product with its name and id

title: In fulfillment, not on the website
what: A Printful product is not linked to any product on your website.
why: It is probably a sample, a draft or a product that was taken off the website. It can still be ordered through Printful's own store.
fix: Delete it in Printful if it is a leftover, or save its id on the website product it belongs to.
tech: a Printful product in matchProducts' unmatchedPrintful; runs only when both Sanity and Printful returned data; one finding per product with its name and id

title: In checkout, not on the website
what: An active Stripe product is not linked to any product on your website.
why: It may be a payment link or an invoice item on purpose. If it is a leftover, it clutters reports and someone may sell it by mistake.
fix: If it is meant to exist, leave it. If not, archive it in Stripe, or save its id on the website product it belongs to.
tech: an active Stripe product in matchProducts' unmatchedStripe; archived ones are skipped; runs only when both Sanity and Stripe returned data, because with no website products read every Stripe product would be unmatched; one finding per product with its name and id

title: A price is stored in two systems
what: The same price is saved on the Sanity product and on the matched Stripe product, and the two agree today.
why: Two copies that agree today are the cause of next month's mismatch: the next price change has to be made twice, and one of them will be forgotten.
fix: Decide which system owns each price, usually checkout, and have the other read it instead of storing its own copy.
tech: a Sanity product with a price whose matched Stripe product has a default price with a fixed amount, in a known currency, equal to it; one finding per run listing the count and the first five products; products whose prices differ are price-mismatch, not this

title: A subscription price in checkout has no plan on the page
what: A Stripe product you listed as a plan has an active subscription price that no plan on the page stands for.
why: A price that is live in Stripe but never shown is either a plan you forgot to put on the site, or an old price that can still be bought from an old link.
fix: Add the plan to the page, or archive the price in Stripe if it should no longer be sold.
tech: for each Stripe product in gaugeline.plans.json products (active), its prices with active true and a recurring object that no plan on the page was matched to; one finding per product listing up to three prices; a product that is archived, or not among the products that were read, says nothing here

title: A field your query asks for is missing on some documents
what: A query asks for a field that some published documents of the type have and others do not.
why: Fine when the field is optional. When the page assumes it is there (a link built from it, an image with no fallback), the documents without it break or show a gap.
fix: If the field is optional, make the template cope with it missing. If it is not, fill it in on the documents listed by their count, or mark it required in the schema.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never counted), asking for count(*[_type == T]) and count(*[_type == T && defined(path)]) for each distinct field path, held in a Map from type to a Map from path to an integer; a reference or an array of objects is counted at the field itself (topic, not topic->title); the answer is integers, so no document and no field value is read; a path whose count is above 0 and below the type's total
